concept.name: Futures commission merchant
concept.definition: A futures commission merchant (FCM) is an individual, association, partnership, corporation, or trust that solicits or accepts orders for the purchase or sale of any commodity for future delivery on or subject to the rules of an exchange and that accepts payment from or extends credit to those whose orders are accepted. FCMs are the futures-industry analogue of carrying brokers and must register with the CFTC (CEA Section 1a(28)).
concept.intuition: An FCM is the futures industry's bank-and-broker combined: it takes your futures orders, holds your margin money, and stands between you and the clearing house.
concept.mechanics: The FCM onboards customers, accepts orders and margin funds, routes trades for execution, and clears them (directly as a clearing member or through one). It must segregate customer funds from firm funds, maintain adjusted net capital, and issue confirmations and statements; introducing brokers without customer-fund handling route their customers to FCMs.
concept.failure_modes: FCM failure puts customer margin at risk when segregation fails, as in the MF Global (2011) and Peregrine (2012) cases where customer funds were misused. Concentration of clearing among few FCMs creates systemic single points of failure.
concept.misconceptions: Customer funds at an FCM are not SIPC-insured like securities accounts; protection rests on CFTC segregation rules, not an insurance backstop. An FCM is also not merely an order-taker — its defining feature is holding customer money.
concept.example: A grain exporter opens a futures account at an FCM, wires $100,000 of margin, and the FCM accepts and clears its hedge orders in corn futures while holding the funds in a segregated customer account.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
